summary: This informational memo describes a way to protect a router's control plane, the part that runs routing protocols and management, from unwanted or malicious traffic. The operator first identifies all legitimate control-plane traffic, then installs a filter in the forwarding path that blocks everything else from reaching the router's brain. It also discusses how to find and maintain that list of legitimate flows.

plainLanguage.summary: A router has a busy brain. This is like putting a guard at its door with a list of allowed visitors, so strangers can't crowd in and stop it from thinking.

questions: how to protect router control plane
how to stop attack traffic reaching a router cpu
subtitle: Filtering unwanted traffic before it reaches the router's control plane

tldr.problem: A router's control plane, which runs routing protocols and management functions, is more susceptible to denial-of-service attacks than the forwarding plane because it runs on general-purpose processors rather than specialized hardware.
tldr.mechanism: Operators identify all legitimate control-plane traffic (routing protocols, management, DNS, NTP, etc.), then install filters and rate limiters in the forwarding plane to block or rate-limit everything else destined to the router itself.
tldr.outcome: The control plane stays stable and responsive even under attack, because unwanted traffic is stopped at the forwarding plane boundary rather than consuming the control plane's processing power.

facts.value: Allowlist approach (explicitly allow known traffic, block the rest)

facts.label: Filter location
facts.value: Forwarding plane (high-speed hardware, not the control plane itself)

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Traffic destined to the router, not traffic passing through it

today: RFC 6192 is an Informational RFC published in March 2011. It remains a widely used guideline for router security configuration; vendors like Cisco and Juniper have incorporated similar control-plane protection mechanisms into their router operating systems.

sections.title: Why Routers Need Control Plane Protection
sections.content:
Modern routers separate their forwarding plane (fast hardware that moves data packets through) from their control plane (software that runs routing protocols and handles management). The forwarding plane is optimized for speed in specialized chips (ASICs) that can handle millions of packets per second. The control plane runs on general-purpose processors and handles all traffic destined to the router itself: routing updates, management commands, DNS queries, and other administrative traffic.

Because the control plane runs on less powerful hardware and manages more complex functions, it is much more vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks than the forwarding plane. If an attacker floods the control plane with unwanted traffic, the router becomes unstable and cannot properly manage its own operations or route packets for others.
sections.plainLanguage: A router is like a postal worker with two jobs: sorting incoming mail (forwarding) and managing the office (control plane). The mail-sorting area is super fast, but the office is slower. If someone floods the office with junk mail, the worker can't get their real work done.

sections.title: Identifying Legitimate Traffic
sections.content:
The method begins by identifying all traffic that the control plane must process. In the example provided, this includes routing protocols (OSPF and BGP from known peers), management access (SSH and SNMP from management stations), time synchronization (NTP), DNS, RADIUS authentication, and ICMP (ping and traceroute). The exact list depends entirely on each network's configuration and operational needs.

Once legitimate traffic is defined, operators can drop or rate-limit everything else. For instance, ICMP traffic might be rate-limited to 500 kbps to allow debugging tools to work while preventing an ICMP flood. Fragmented packets can be dropped because the control plane should never receive fragments. Unknown traffic can be rate-limited to 500 kbps or dropped completely, depending on operational requirements and risk tolerance.
sections.plainLanguage: First, the guard makes a list of everyone who should visit the office: coworkers, clients, delivery people. Then, the guard turns away anyone else or limits how many strangers can visit per hour.

sections.title: Installing Filters in the Forwarding Plane
sections.content:
The filters are deployed not at the control plane itself, but in the forwarding plane. Because the forwarding plane operates in high-speed hardware, it can filter traffic with minimal performance impact, and the filtering happens before traffic consumes the limited resources of the control plane. The filter counts every packet it matches, providing valuable forensic data about attacks or anomalies.

Filters explicitly define allowed traffic (by IP address, protocol, port, or subnet), specify what to do with each class of traffic (permit, rate-limit, or drop), and then drop all remaining traffic not explicitly allowed. This allowlist approach is more secure than a blocklist approach because it defaults to protecting the control plane if new threats emerge.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard checks people at the door (in the fast lane) before they reach the office, not at the office itself. The guard keeps count of every visitor to help spot trouble.

sections.title: Trade-Offs: Protection vs. Operability
sections.content:
Tight protection comes with costs. For example, completely blocking ICMP prevents ping and traceroute, which are essential debugging tools. Blocking IP fragments protects against certain attacks but may break legitimate protocols. Filtering IP options stops one class of attack but may break Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) if your network uses it. Operators must balance attack prevention against the risk of breaking legitimate operations.

The RFC recommends starting with a permissive policy that allows all traffic initially, then monitoring what actually reaches the control plane before deploying strict filters. This allows operators to identify legitimate traffic they might have missed. Counters on each filter class provide forensic data: high counters on a filter catching normal traffic suggest a misconfiguration, while high counters on the default class suggest unknown legitimate traffic or an attack in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: A stricter guard list means fewer unwanted visitors, but it also risks turning away people who should be let in. Good guards audit and adjust their list as they learn what the office really needs.

sections.title: What This Protection Does and Doesn't Do
sections.content:
Control plane protection filters traffic destined to the router itself, not traffic passing through it. Routers also need edge protection (filtering at network borders) to stop spoofed packets and other attacks from ever reaching your network. The filters do not protect against cryptographic attacks on protocols like BGP or SNMP; those protocols should use their own security methods (authentication, encryption).

Some special cases need extra thought: ICMP rate limiting may drop legitimate ICMP during an attack, TTL-expired traffic needs protection to prevent control-plane overload from generating ICMP Time Exceeded messages, and router-generated ICMP replies must themselves be rate-limited. IPv6 adds complexity because ICMPv6 is not optional—it handles Neighbor Discovery and other essential functions, so ICMPv6 filtering must be more permissive than IPv4 ICMP filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard at the control plane door helps, but you also need guards at the building entrance to check packages before they arrive. And the guard's list doesn't protect against someone showing fake credentials—protocols need their own secret passwords.
